node.label: Wendy Brown
node.date_label: “Wounded Attachments” (1993) · States of Injury (1995) · Is Critique Secular?, with Asad, Butler and Mahmood (2009) · Undoing the Demos (2015) · In the Ruins of Neoliberalism (2019) · Nihilistic Times (2023)
node.description: A political theorist of power, freedom and neoliberal reason. Undoing the Demos (2015) treats neoliberalism as a governing rationality rather than a set of policies, a form of reason that extends the model of the market to every domain of life and de-democratizes the state; Brown says Foucault, among others, taught this way of thinking. Her essay “Wounded Attachments” (1993) preceded States of Injury (1995), which includes a chapter of that title and, in its publisher’s description, offers a sympathetic critique of identity politics that asks how woundedness became a basis for political identity, drawing on Nietzsche, Marx, Weber and Foucault. In her introduction to Is Critique Secular? (2009) she traced how Marx’s distinction between criticism and critique bound critique to secularism in Western critical theory; Judith Butler took up that distinction in the same volume. Daniel T. Rodgers (2018) used Undoing the Demos to illustrate the most enveloping use of “neoliberalism”, arguing that so stretched a term, and Brown’s language of exhaustion and collapse, may make a workable politics harder to see. In the Ruins of Neoliberalism (2019) reads Hayek’s joining of markets and traditional morality as a source of antidemocratic politics; Matthew McManus (2020) found its Nietzschean final chapter neglected religious questions of meaning. Nihilistic Times (2023) returns to Weber’s lectures on scholarship and politics as vocations.
node.representative_figures_and_works: “Wounded Attachments,” Political Theory 21, no. 3 (1993): 390–410; States of Injury: Power and Freedom in Late Modernity (1995); Is Critique Secular? Blasphemy, Injury, and Free Speech (2009, with Talal Asad, Judith Butler and Saba Mahmood; Brown’s introduction); Walled States, Waning Sovereignty (2010); Undoing the Demos: Neoliberalism’s Stealth Revolution (2015); In the Ruins of Neoliberalism: The Rise of Antidemocratic Politics in the West (2019); Nihilistic Times: Thinking with Max Weber (2023).
node.scope_note: Brown’s 2009 introduction and the 2022 interview were read in full; Rodgers’s 2018 essay and the reviews by McManus (2020) and Moyn (2024) were read in full. The books are unread: States of Injury is described from its publisher’s page, Undoing the Demos from Brown’s interview and Rodgers’s essay, In the Ruins of Neoliberalism and Nihilistic Times from one review each. Several pages were read in web-archive captures of permitted pages because the live pages returned 403. For “Wounded Attachments” (1993), the journal metadata and displayed notes were read; the main article text remains unread.

chronology.interpretation: Argument claims rest on Brown’s 2009 introduction, her 2022 interview, a publisher description and three readers (Rodgers, McManus, Moyn), with reading limits recorded on each edge.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Uses and Abuses of ‘Neoliberalism’” (2018) Rodgers takes Brown’s Undoing the Demos (2015) as the exemplar of the most enveloping use of the term, neoliberalism as a governing rationality, and argues that its language of exhaustion and collapse, and categories stretched so wide, may make a workable politics harder to see.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete essay read in a Wayback capture of Dissent’s own page. Paragraph beginning “Neoliberalism (4), the latest entry into this parade”: “In the terms Wendy Brown takes from Foucault in her witheringly critical Undoing the Demos (2015), neoliberalism is … the ‘governing rationality’ of our times.” Paragraph beginning “Many of those who have written most acutely”: Brown is quoted on neoliberalism as “inconstant” and “plastic”. Paragraph beginning “At its extreme, bundling the ills”: “There is grit in her Undoing the Demos. But a language of pessimism … runs through it … Or perhaps it is that the distended categories make a workable politics all the harder to perceive.” Rodgers also calls her “one of the leading public intellectual activists of our day”: a respectful but pointed critique. Brown did not respond in the Dissent forum that followed; her response, if any, was not sought.

proposed_edges.relationship: In a 2022 Dissent interview Brown says that Foucault, among others, taught her generation to think of neoliberalism not as a set of policies but as a form of governmental reason that shapes conduct across every dimension of life; Daniel T. Rodgers (2018) likewise describes Undoing the Demos (2015) as using terms Brown takes from Foucault.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Interview, Brown’s first answer, paragraph beginning “Foucault, among others, taught us to think about neoliberalism as more than a set of policies, and rather as a form of governmental reason.” Rodgers (2018), paragraph beginning “Neoliberalism (4)”: “In the terms Wendy Brown takes from Foucault”. Brown’s own words (“taught us”) state the debt as shared, not as hers alone. Undoing the Demos and its chapter on Foucault’s lectures are unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her introduction to Is Critique Secular? (2009) Brown argues that Marx’s distinction between “mere criticism” of religion and critique of the conditions that produce it is the move that bound critique to secularism in Western critical theory, a heritage she says the volume’s question upends.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Brown’s introduction, complete. P. 10, section “Uncritical Secularism”: “we must consider Marx’s own development of critique out of what he took to be the shortcomings of the Young Hegelians’ critical approach to religion … This is the move that really secures the conviction that critique is secular in the Western critical theory tradition.” Pp. 10–11 expound Marx (n. 5–6, Contribution to the Critique of Hegel’s Philosophy of Right, Introduction). Pp. 11–12: “It is this particular heritage from Marx, and the way it threads through German critical theory right up through Habermas, that has so overdetermined the imbrication … of critique with secularism”; p. 12: the question “upends one of critical theory’s founding planks”. A genealogical critique of what critical theory inherited from Marx, not a rejection of Marx’s analysis as such.

proposed_edges.relationship: Brown’s introduction to Is Critique Secular? (2009) draws on Koselleck’s Critique and Crisis (1959; cited in the 1988 English translation) for its history of the word: critique emerging in ancient Athens as the jurisprudential krisis and narrowing as it passed into Latin and the European vernaculars.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction, p. 8, section “Critique . . .”: “From Reinhart Kosellek’s Critique and Crisis, we learn that critique emerges in ancient Athens as the jurisprudential term krisis” (name so spelled in the text), followed by a paraphrase of Koselleck’s account; n. 2 cites Critique and Crisis (1988 English edition) and notes that Asad offers a different etymology. A body-text use of Koselleck’s argument in one section of a short introduction; no broader debt claimed.
proposed_edges.map_label: Koselleck’s krisis in Brown’s genealogy of critique

proposed_edges.relationship: Brown’s work draws on Nietzsche from States of Injury (1995), which its publisher says weaves Nietzsche together with Marx, Weber and Foucault to analyse how woundedness became a basis for political identity, to the final chapter of In the Ruins of Neoliberalism (2019), which a reviewer describes as working on a Nietzschean basis to return to the politics of resentment.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Princeton description of States of Injury (Wayback capture): “She also develops an original theoretical practice that weaves together Nietzsche, Marx, Weber, Foucault, and cultural theories of gender and race”. McManus, Radical Philosophy 208 (2020), paragraph beginning “The book’s last chapter returns Brown to the politics of resentment she has been probing since States of Injury decades ago”: “Chapter Five operates on a more Nietzschean basis”; paragraph beginning “Brown´s reading in this concluding chapter”: “crucial as Nietzsche is to her work”, with McManus’s criticism that she largely ignores religious concerns about transcendent meaning. Publisher description and a reviewer’s account; neither book read, and “Wounded Attachments” (1993) not reached.
proposed_edges.map_label: Nietzsche and the politics of ressentiment

proposed_edges.relationship: In her response in Is Critique Secular? (2009) Butler adopts the distinction between critique and criticism that Brown drew in the volume’s introduction, and credits Brown with showing that Marx’s formulation of critique has its own history in religious metaphor and structure.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Butler, “The Sensibility of Critique: Response to Asad and Mahmood”, p. 107, section “Criticism, Critique, and Formations of the Subject”: “As Wendy Brown has pointed out in the introduction to this volume, the distinction between ‘critique’ and ‘criticism’ is an important one. I would gloss that distinction in the following way”. P. 125: “the formulation of critique in Marx is not, as Wendy Brown has shown, without its own history and legacy in religious metaphor and structure”, n. 20 citing Brown, “The Sacred, the Secular, and the Profane: Charles Taylor and Karl Marx” (2009, forthcoming). Body-text engagement in a co-authored volume; the four authors’ co-credit itself is not counted as the relationship. The cited Brown essay is unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Butler takes up Brown’s critique/criticism distinction

proposed_edges.relationship: States of Injury (1995), in its publisher’s description, offers a sympathetic critique of identity politics, exploring how woundedness became a basis for contemporary political identity and how the conditions that formed such identities constrain emancipatory desire.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Princeton description: “A sympathetic critique that attempts to free Left politics from its own snares, States of Injury explores how woundedness became a basis for contemporary political identity. Without condemning identity politics, Wendy Brown carefully probes the varied historical forces generating them today and the ways these formative conditions constrain emancipatory desire.” McManus (2020) confirms that she has been probing the politics of resentment “since States of Injury”. Publisher description only; the book is unread. The edge concerns identity politics as a political form, which the atlas node treats under Hunt’s “identity politics” grouping; it does not claim a critique of historians’ identity histories.

proposed_edges.relationship: Opening a Berkeley critical theory programme meant to bridge European and non-Western critical theory, Brown’s introduction to Is Critique Secular? (2009) argues that the identification of critique with secularism, inherited from Marx and threaded through German critical theory up to Habermas, is one of critical theory’s founding planks, and that the volume’s question upends it.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction, p. 7: the symposium was “the inaugural public event for a new research and teaching program in critical theory at Berkeley, a program that aims to bridge conventional divides between modern European critical theory and non-Western and post-Enlightenment critical theoretical projects”. Pp. 11–12: the Marx heritage “threads through German critical theory right up through Habermas”; p. 12: “this question upends one of critical theory’s founding planks”, while allowing “other formulations of critique”. Context: McManus (2020) notes her use of Marcuse’s “repressive desublimation” in In the Ruins of Neoliberalism; the 2022 interview defines critical theory broadly. A critique from within critical theory, not a rejection of it.

proposed_edges.relationship: Nihilistic Times: Thinking with Max Weber (2023) is, in Samuel Moyn’s review, a meditation on Weber’s lectures on scholarship and politics as vocations that argues for a critical retrieval of Weber’s insistence on separating scholarship from politics, while staying wary of his longing for charismatic leadership.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Moyn, Critical Inquiry, 1 February 2024 (one-paragraph review): “Wendy Brown’s exquisite meditation on Max Weber’s classic lectures on knowledge and politics as vocations”; “Sensibly, Brown argues for a critical retrieval of Weber’s insistence on the isolation of scholarship from politics, though on different grounds”; “Brown insists on much more wariness of Weber’s inchoate longing for charismatic leadership”. Moyn doubts that the present is as close to Weber’s world as Brown suggests. A reviewer’s account; the book (published in the Tanner Lectures on Human Values series, per search listings) is unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: A critical retrieval of Weber’s vocation lectures

proposed_edges.relationship: In the abstract for his lecture ‘Seeing Red: Recognition, Reconciliation & Resentment in Indigenous Politics’ (2012), Glen Coulthard challenges the argument he attributes to Wendy Brown and Saul Newman that ressentiment risks reproducing emancipatory movements’ powerlessness, arguing instead that resentment can be legitimate and politically transformative under continuing colonial domination.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete lecture abstract on Fernwood Publishing’s own event page. It explicitly attributes the powerlessness argument to Brown and Newman, announces an engagement with that argument, and presents Coulthard’s contrary claims about the legitimacy and transformative possibilities of resentment. This is an abstract-level critique, not evidence that the lecture recording or Red Skin, White Masks (2014) was read. The abstract does not identify a particular Brown publication, so none is supplied here. The event header and body differ over the January day; both give 2012, the only date used in the relationship. The claim concerns published political scholarship only; no community knowledge or personal identity information is reproduced.

proposed_edges.relationship: Regulating Aversion: Tolerance in the Age of Identity and Empire (2006), as described by its publisher, contributes to postcolonial critique by arguing that tolerance discourse can distinguish a civilized West from a barbaric Islam and thereby justify Western imperial violence.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher description and bibliographic information in Google Books’ record of the 2006 Princeton University Press edition; also checked the description in its 2009 edition record. The description specifically connects tolerance’s civilizational hierarchy to the Iraq war, the War on Terror, and imperialism. The book’s chapters were not read. Assignment to the existing Postcolonial history / critique endpoint is an editorial mapping of this specific argument, not a claim that the source calls Brown a member of a school or establishes reception by particular historians. This is distinct from the input’s existing identity-politics and critical-theory pairs.
